title: GDPR and Security Cameras: What European Homeowners Must Know
excerpt: A doorbell that films the pavement can make you a data controller under GDPR. Lenses, signs, storage limits and neighbour requests, explained plainly.
author: HiddenCameras Editorial Team
authorBio: The HiddenCameras.tv editorial team researches and writes about security cameras, surveillance technology, and home safety.
body:
The surprise most European homeowners meet too late: the moment your doorbell records the pavement, the shared driveway, or a neighbour's door, data-protection law is likely to treat you as a data controller — responsible for other people's personal information, with duties to match. A camera on your own hallway is one thing; a lens sweeping the street is legally a different device. This guide explains where that line falls and what to do about aiming, signs, storage, and requests. Rules are applied country by country, so treat this as general information and check your own national authority's guidance.

Why footage of strangers counts as personal data at all

Under Europe's data-protection framework, any information relating to an identifiable person is personal data — a clear face, a licence plate, even a recognisable gait qualifies. Running a camera that captures such images means you are processing personal data, which brings plain duties: collect only what you need, keep it no longer than necessary, keep it secure, and be transparent. Think of the camera as the law does — a small filing system for images of other people — then make proportionate choices about aim, signs, and storage.

The household exemption ends where the public begins

There is a widely misunderstood carve-out for purely household activity — the family album, the phone contacts list. For a camera filming only inside your own home, that reading is usually right. But courts in Europe have held that when a home camera also monitors public space — street, pavement, communal stairwell — the exemption no longer covers that outward-facing recording. So angle every camera to include as little public space as the job allows, use masking or activity zones to black out neighbours' windows and doors, and note why the remaining coverage is necessary. A doorbell must catch some pavement; a garden camera has no excuse for framing the neighbour's patio.

Aiming the lens: pavements, shared drives, and neighbours' doors

Walk outside and look at what each camera actually frames — most people are surprised by how much street and neighbour ends up in shot.

The doorbell's pavement problem

Stand where visitors stand and note how much street, parked car, and opposite house appears behind them. Tilt or wedge the unit so the frame centres on your doorway and path, and mask the rest. Some pavement in frame is unavoidable; the point is to show you minimised it on purpose.

Shared drives and disputed wide shots

Check garden and driveway cameras the same way — height widens the frame into neighbouring plots. If you share a driveway, agree positions with neighbours before finalising; a camera everyone accepted generates no complaints, while one discovered later generates formal ones. A narrower lens or a moved mount almost always resolves disagreement, and a disputed wide shot is rarely worth the conflict.

Signs and transparency: telling people they are filmed

People being recorded should be able to find out who is recording and why — normally a small sign at the boundary of the monitored area, stating that recording is in progress, who operates the camera, and how to contact them. Many national authorities publish example wording worth copying. Keep a short note for yourself too: why each camera exists, what it covers, how long you keep footage. Written before any complaint, that note turns an awkward argument into a calm explanation.

How long to keep footage, and how to keep it safe

Keep recordings only as long as the purpose needs, then let them be overwritten — for most homes a rolling window of days, not an archive of months. Anything longer needs a reason you could explain out loud. Protect what you hold: a strong unique password with two-factor authentication, updated software, and care over who in the household can view and share clips. Think twice before posting footage of strangers online, even after an incident; publishing an identifiable person creates problems beyond the original trespass. If footage is needed as evidence, save a copy and hand it to the police rather than publishing it.

When a neighbour asks — or complains

Requests come in two flavours. An access request — someone believes your camera caught them — gets a check of what you hold and a timely share that protects other people's privacy in the frame. An objection — a neighbour says your camera watches their property — gets a serious re-check: re-aim, apply masking, narrow the field, and reply explaining what changed. Most disputes end there. If not, the neighbour may approach your national data-protection authority, and your earlier notes, signage, and careful aiming become your defence. Households with no sign, no masking, and no written reason fare worst — fix those three this weekend. For rented property, see our guide on landlord cameras and tenant rights.

General information only: data-protection rules are interpreted and enforced differently across European countries, and national guidance changes. Check your own data-protection authority's homeowner advice for your jurisdiction, and get local legal advice before relying on any general guide for a dispute.
